title: AI Helps You Refinance, Mortgages Get Pricier
dek: Cheap US mortgages partly rely on most borrowers being too lazy to refinance when rates drop. Once AI agents remind everyone to refinance promptly, that option gets repriced and mortgage rates actually rise.
why: This episode pushes the consequences of 'AI removing friction' to the extreme: the money you think you save gets repriced away by the financial system. The second half covers phantom bidding in Amazon's ad auction and ETF dividend timing trades.
who: People in mortgages, asset management, law firm management, ad auction operations, and any founder concerned with how AI removing friction changes financial product pricing.
skip: Skip the first about 4 minutes of small talk and introductions; from minute 5, when the AI refinancing topic starts, there are essentially no filler segments.

points.h: AI reminders to refinance make mortgages more expensive
points.body: US homeowners generally don't act when rates drop: Matt met someone on a plane who was boasting about his mortgage rate and planning to sell and upsize, and Matt talked him out of it. Morgan Stanley research suggests that if AI agents remind you to refinance when rates drop 200 basis points, future refinancing will be much easier. Sounds like saving you money, but more frequent refinancing means the prepayment option people previously 'couldn't be bothered to exercise' actually gets exercised, lenders reprice for that, and everyone's mortgage rate rises by 10 to 20 basis points.

points.h: Smarter homeowners mean fewer people can buy
points.body: Fabrice Touré—former head of mortgage derivatives at Goldman Sachs, now a finance academic—writes plainly: policies that make refinancing more frequent also raise equilibrium mortgage rates and reduce the likelihood that a large number of borrowers get credit. The reason is that the US 30-year fixed-rate, prepayable mortgage carries an expensive option, but most borrowers exercise it poorly, which is why lenders are willing to price rates lower. Once institutions or AI make everyone more rational, the option gets repriced, rates rise, and fewer people who were implicitly subsidized by the low rate can afford homes.

points.h: Models priced on past behavior will trip
points.body: The shock hits investors first. Morgan Stanley warns that historical prepayment behavior will underestimate future prepayments: any model trained on past data misprices 'borrowers being more willing to exercise their prepayment option.' As a result, some mortgage-related assets look cheap but are actually built on the assumption that borrowers stay lazy; when AI compresses refinancing friction from two weeks to ten minutes, those assets need a full repricing. Matt extends the logic: credit card points, high-yield savings accounts, life insurance policies—the financial system largely runs on customers not using every option to the fullest.

points.h: AI makes the billable hour model obsolete
points.body: The squeeze on professional services shows up first in law firms: clients think AI can do the work of a squad of junior associates and demand lower fees. Firms bill by the hour on the surface, but the real profit comes from partners selling junior associates' hours at a high rate and paying them a lower wage; if AI does the bulk of the grunt work, 'billing for junior associate hours' no longer holds. Senior lawyers' judgment is still valuable, but it needs a different pricing model. The bigger problem: when juniors no longer spend hundreds of hours on basic work, where do the future partners develop their instincts?

points.h: Top partners can go solo with AI
points.body: Since a senior lawyer's value isn't realized through headcount, the very best will do the math first: rather than stay at a big platform to support the partner committee and train a cohort of juniors, they'll leave and open a boutique with just themselves and six AI agents. Chris Kircher, a former Quinn Emanuel partner, has already resigned to start an AI-native firm built around that bet. If enough senior people leave, big firms can't retain them even knowing the apprenticeship model matters—the revenue-generating capacity walks out, the money-losing training system stays, and the big firm struggles to survive.

points.h: Amazon's auction has a hidden bidder
points.body: The FTC and 22 state attorneys general are suing Amazon, saying its ad auction isn't the second-price auction it's advertised to be. In a normal second-price auction, the highest bidder pays the second-highest bid; Amazon instead adds a 'soft reserve'—the platform's own valuation of the ad slot, like a bidder hiding in the shadows. If your bid is above the soft reserve, the soft reserve becomes the second price; if your bid is below it, the winner pays their own maximum bid. Amazon's response: the ad auction is a real-time black box by design, no one can know the soft reserve in advance, and advertisers just look at return on ad spend.

points.h: Bidding at the chandelier is legal
points.body: Finance forbids exchanges from secretly placing buy orders for themselves, but art auction houses have a legal performance. The seller sets a confidential reserve, and when live bids don't reach it, the auctioneer calls out bids into empty space, pushing the price up to the reserve—the term is 'chandelier bid,' because he often looks up at the chandelier. New York requires auction catalogs to disclose: the auctioneer may bid on behalf of the seller up to the reserve, and won't indicate which bids come from the seller. Amazon's soft reserve is similarly the platform bidding for itself, but without such a fine-print disclosure of the rules—that's exactly what the FTC is seizing on.

Foreign funds (e.g., Cayman structures) pay withholding tax on US stock dividends, which drags on the thin margins of basis trades. Some in the market use two nearly identical S&P 500 ETFs with a timing difference: BlackRock's IVV and Vanguard's VOO have ex-dividend dates about a week apart. The maneuver: sell IVV before its ex-date and switch into VOO; then switch back when VOO is about to pay. After the ex-date, the fund price drops by roughly the dividend amount, so the investor avoids the taxed dividend and earns the same amount back by selling high and buying low. This is an institutional tax strategy; retail investors copying it would generate large capital gains taxes—not a TikTok money tip.

terms.def: The highest bidder wins but pays only the second-highest bid.

An auctioneer bids on behalf of the seller into empty air to push the price toward the reserve; named because he often looks up at the chandelier.
Simultaneously buying the spot asset and selling the future to capture the spread; essentially providing funding.
